text: Millions of fires are reported across the world every year. If you don't have a plan, then get out a pen. Here's how to survive a fire The main causes of housefires are all preventable. For the most part, we're simply not paying attention. We're either distracted, or we're just not being careful. An unattended stove, a lit cigarette, a faulty appliance. We've all had a few close calls; burned into our memory, never to be repeated. But have you really learned your lesson? Fires are unpredictable, but your survival doesn't have to be.

text: There's stress, there's confusion, there's a lot of heat, but no matter what, you've gotta stay cool. And the best way to do that is knowing what to do. Plan a few escape routes and get familiar with them. It's always nice to have a few options that can get you out calmly, quickly, and safely.

video_title: How to Survive a Fire, According to Science
text: Your room, or your home, will start filling up with smoke very quickly, and chances are, you're going to have to pass through it in order to get out. Breathing in too much smoke can cause you to pass out. But you can fight back by wetting a cloth and holding it over your nose and mouth. Covering your nose and mouth might only buy you a few extra minutes, but in life and death, every second counts. And while smoke may be a greater threat than the fire itself, it also rises. So on top of protecting your nose and mouth, you can improve your chances by getting on your hands and knees, and crawling your way towards an exit.

video_title: How to Survive a Fire, According to Science
text: In a house fire, a closed door can either save you or stop you in your tracks. As you pass from one room to another, remember to close doors behind you to help prevent the fire from spreading any faster. Fires need oxygen to survive, so by closing doors, you're cutting off the free flow of oxygen between rooms. By the same token, be careful when you open doors ahead of you. Look for any smoke that might be coming through the cracks, and feel the door itself for heat. You don't want to open it if there's a fire raging on the other side. If the door feels okay, then open it just a crack, to make sure. If the room's clear, move ahead, but stay alert.
